children.text: This small bay in Zambales has a grey beach formed by ash deposited during the

eruption of Mount Pinatubo, with a pine-like agoho forest growing on top of it. It's a well-known camping spot where you pitch a tent on a beach with almost no electricity or mobile signal and spend the night under the stars.
Anawangin Cove is a small bay reached by boat, about
30–45 minutes

south along the coast from Pundaquit, a fishing village in San Antonio, Zambales Province. Grass-covered mountain ridges stretch down to the sea on both sides, enclosing the bay, making it a semi-isolated beach reachable overland only by crossing the mountains.
The scenery here is quite different from a typical tropical Philippine beach. The sand isn't white but a silvery grey, said to have formed from ash that poured out when Mount Pinatubo erupted in

and sediment that later washed down the rivers and settled on the coast. Instead of palm trees, a dense forest of agoho (ironwood) stands behind the beach, its slender needle-like leaves drooping down, and first-time visitors often mistake it for "a beach with a pine forest." Behind the forest, a freshwater stream flowing down from the mountains meets the sea to form a small lagoon.
There is no village at Anawangin, and mobile signal is weak or nonexistent. Destinare Beach Resort & Campsite at the southern end of the bay runs a generator to supply power only during the hours of
4 PM–8 AM

; the other campsites have almost no electricity. Most travelers spend the night in a tent pitched in the shade of the agoho forest or in a simple rented hut, listening to the waves and stargazing by the campfire. Thanks to this rustic charm, it has been a go-to beach camping spot for young people from Manila and camping clubs since the late

It suits travelers who love camping and the outdoors, groups of friends or club members, and anyone wanting a digital detox away from the city. Amenities are limited, so if you'd prefer a comfortable resort holiday, it's better to stay at a beach resort in Pundaquit or San Antonio and visit as a day trip.
Of the many coves lining the west coast of the Redondo Peninsula in southern Zambales, Anawangin is the closest to Pundaquit. To the south along the coast lie Talisayen Cove,
Nagsasa Cove
and Silanguin Cove, while
Capones and Camara Islands

sit just off Pundaquit. That's why the most common ways to visit are on a day island-hopping trip that takes in these islands and coves one after another by boat, or by camping overnight at Anawangin and touring the nearby islands the next morning on the way back.

Pitching a tent in the forest shade right behind the beach and spending the night there is the heart of a trip to Anawangin. Sunlight filtering through the trees at dusk and the stars in the night sky create an unforgettable scene.
It takes
15–20 minutes

to climb the roughly 270 steps up the hill at the southern end of the bay, and from the top you can take in the half-moon beach, the agoho forest, the blue sea and even the empty cove next door all at once. A fee of about
per person is charged at the entrance, and photos are best in the early morning or at dusk.
Capones Island, off the coast of Pundaquit, still has a brick lighthouse built in the late Spanish colonial period. Get off the boat and climb a rocky path for
15–20 minutes
and the lighthouse and an open sweep of sea unfold before you.
A narrow sandbar that appears at low tide, connecting two islands, great for swimming and photos.
A wider, quieter bay south of Anawangin, also with volcanic-ash sand and an agoho forest. Island hopping packages combining both spots are popular.
Walk along the stream and lagoon behind the beach to see the distinctive landscape where sea, forest, and mountain meet. It's also good for a quick rinse after swimming in saltwater.
A route to Anawangin over the mountains instead of by boat, walking along grassy ridges with sea views. Recommended for those with fitness and experience, and a guide is essential.

A small bay south of Anawangin with the same silvery-grey sand and agoho forest, but it gets few visitors, so it stays quiet even in the peak summer season. It's often included in day hopping trips covering four spots: Camara Island, Nagsasa, Talisayen and Anawangin (about
per boat for up to 4 people).

There are no reliable water sources and almost no shade on the trail, so carry 2–3 liters of water per person and set off before sunrise. Hiking alone is not allowed, so hire a guide in Pundaquit; it's also common to hand your heavy gear in advance to the boat that will pick you up the next day.
From Manila, take NLEX up and switch to SCTEX, exit at Tipo, pass through Subic and Olongapo, and follow the Zambales coastal road north for about
1 hour
to reach San Antonio. It's about
180km
, taking
4–5 hours
. From San Antonio to Pundaquit is about
5km
. Paid parking is available at homes and resorts around Pundaquit beach.
An environmental fee of
per person is collected as you enter Pundaquit, and parking near the beach costs around
per night for a car and around
for a motorcycle.

4–5 hours
, and the fare is about

15 minutes
by tricycle, at about
per tricycle.

, about

Hire a boat (bangka) at Pundaquit beach; the ride takes about
30–45 minutes
. There are no scheduled ferries, and every trip means chartering a whole boat. In a boat for up to 4 people, a round trip to Anawangin only costs about
, adding Capones and Camara Islands about
, and a day hopping trip to four spots including Nagsasa Cove about

; larger groups can hire a bigger boat and pay less per person. If you're staying overnight, agree on an exact pickup time for the next day and get the captain's contact number. Fares are negotiated based on group size, stops and season.
Walking over the mountains from Pundaquit to Anawangin takes about
3–5 hours
. The grassy ridge has almost no shade, so a pre-dawn start and a local guide are essential.

The west coast of Zambales, where Anawangin lies, has sharply distinct dry and wet seasons. In the
November–May
dry season there's little rain and the sea is calm, making both boat trips and camping easy. Average rainfall in nearby Iba stays at 21mm or less a month in
December–March
, but rises to 247mm in
May
, when showers become frequent in the latter part of the month. In
December–February
, night temperatures drop to around
, making it the most comfortable time for camping, while in
March–May
the sea is warm and daytime highs reach
, great for swimming and stargazing.
During the
June–October

wet season, the southwest monsoon (Habagat) blows straight in from the sea, bringing high waves and frequent heavy rain. The coast guard often bans small boats from operating, and the campsite sometimes closes. It's best to avoid visiting during this period.
On weekends during Holy Week and summer vacation (
March–May
), the campsite fills up densely with tents, making it hard to feel a quiet atmosphere. Go on a weekday or during the off-peak dry season (
November
January–February
) and you'll find a far quieter Anawangin.

There are no hotels at Anawangin; most people stay in tents or simple rented huts. The exception is Destinare Beach Resort & Campsite at the southern end of the bay, which has tepee tents, nipa huts, air-conditioned villas, a swimming pool and a restaurant, and charges an entrance fee separate from the room rate. If you don't bring a tent you can rent one on site, but numbers are limited, so bring your own in peak season. If you'd rather stay in comfort, base yourself at a beach resort in Pundaquit (about
a night) and visit Anawangin on a day hopping trip. Many Pundaquit resorts can also arrange boats and hopping packages.

You can buy snacks, drinks and ice at the campsite stores, and Destinare Resort has a restaurant, but the menu is small and prices are high, so most people bring their own food. It's common to buy rice, meat or fish for grilling, fruit and ice at Pundaquit beach and the San Antonio public market and pack them in a cooler. Follow the campsite management's instructions on where fires are allowed and the rules for them.
Zambales is famous for having the sweetest mangoes in the Philippines; in
, a carabao mango from here entered the Guinness World Records as the world's sweetest mango. If you visit during the
April–May
mango season, be sure to try ripe carabao mangoes at the San Antonio or Iba markets. Every
April
, the provincial capital Iba hosts the Dinamulag mango festival, which in
ran for three days,
April 10–12
. On the way back, seafood restaurants and American-style barbecue joints await in Olongapo and Subic.
There are few ATMs in San Antonio and Pundaquit, and they often run out of cash. Have all your money ready in cash for the boat, entrance fee, and food.
Mobile signal is weak and only reaches parts of the campsite. Let your family know your itinerary and boat return time in advance.
There's no electricity, so bring plenty of power banks, a headlamp, and spare batteries.
Bring at least 3 liters of drinking water per person per day. Use the campsite's pump water only for washing.
Shaded spots in the agoho forest fill up fast. Arrive before
10 AM
and you can pick a good spot.
The sand is fine and blows into your tent when the wind picks up. Bring long tent stakes suited for sand and a waterproof ground sheet.
Boat fares are negotiable, but boats hired cheaply sometimes don't come back at the agreed return time. Book through a trustworthy resort or a registered boat association.
The rule is to carry out all your trash. Bring several large trash bags.

The resorts and boat operators in Pundaquit sell overnight packages bundling the round-trip boat, entrance fee, Capones Island hopping, a shared tent, and drinking water. The more people, the cheaper it gets, at about
per person, so for a small group without gear it can be more convenient and cheaper than renting things separately.
The forest campsites get a lot of mosquitoes from dusk. Bring insect repellent and thin long-sleeved clothing.
Winds pick up in the afternoon and waves get higher. Take the return boat before noon if possible, and follow the captain's judgment on days with high waves.
Anawangin's beach drops off steeply, so the water gets deep after just a few steps in. There are no lifeguards, so children and weak swimmers should wear a life vest.
During the wet season and typhoon warnings, the coast guard bans boats from departing. Don't push your way in on an unlicensed boat.
The sand gets very hot at midday, and UV exposure is strong outside the shade. Guard against heatstroke and sunburn.
There have been cases of lost belongings at the campsite. It's best to keep valuables on your person or not bring them at all.
Only build fires and cook in designated areas. The dry agoho forest catches fire easily.

There is no clinic in the bay. If you get injured or sick, you'll have to call a boat to get back to Pundaquit, so bring basic medicines and a first-aid kit, and be sure to get the captain's contact number.

1–1.5 hours
by boat from Pundaquit. A wider, quieter volcanic-ash sand beach and agoho forest than Anawangin.

by boat from Pundaquit. Two islands with a Spanish-era brick lighthouse first lit in

by car. A former U.S. naval base where you can enjoy jungle experiences, a marine theme park, and wreck diving.

3 hours
by car. The emerald crater lake of the very volcano that created Anawangin's sand.

by car. A surf beach town in northern Zambales where you can take beginner surf lessons when the waves are good.
